title: A 3D PINN-Based Framework for Patient-Specific Pulmonary Hemodynamics Using Windkessel Models
authors: Celia Taboada, Luis Nuñez, Angélica Casero, Pedro Navas
abstract: Cardiovascular fluid dynamics modeling relies heavily on mesh-based numerical methods such as Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD). While accurate, these methods entail significant computational costs and complex meshing workflows that limit their translation to clinical practice. Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) are a promising meshless alternative that embeds the governing equations directly into neural network training. In this work, we propose a PINN framework for pulsatile blood flow in patient-specific geometries with dynamic lumped-parameter Windkessel (RCR) outlet conditions representing distal vascular impedance. Coupling the Windkessel ODE to a 3D network raises two difficulties: the ODE alone does not fix the pressure level, and the local pressure variations that drive the flow are orders of magnitude smaller than the basal pressure imposed by the outlet. We address them by decomposing pressure into a time-dependent basal part and a spatially varying part, an initial condition and gauge for the Windkessel equation, a global mass-balance constraint, and a periodic Fourier embedding of time. Validated on 2D canonical channels (steady and pulsatile, with and without RCR outlet), the framework is then applied to a patient-specific right pulmonary artery, reproducing outlet flow, mean pressure, and the velocity and dynamic pressure fields with errors on the order of the data resolution. Finally, we solve the inverse problem of identifying the three Windkessel parameters of the outlet from synthetic data, recovering them with errors of about 0.3% from deliberately wrong initial values. Residual biases in the local pressure field and the need to test robustness to noisy clinical data remain open, but the results support PINNs as complementary tools for meshless hemodynamics and patient-specific digital twins.

infographic.key_insight: A 3D physics-informed neural network couples patient-specific pulmonary blood flow with Windkessel outlet dynamics by separating basal pressure from smaller spatial pressure variations.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework supports meshless hemodynamic prediction and outlet-parameter estimation for patient-specific digital twins.
method: Embed flow equations and dynamic Windkessel (RCR) outlet conditions in PINN training.
Separate pressure components and enforce a Windkessel initial condition, pressure gauge, and global mass balance.
Use periodic Fourier time embedding to represent pulsatile flow.
infographic.evidence_signal: Tests on canonical 2D channels and a patient-specific right pulmonary artery showed flow-field errors on the order of data resolution; inverse estimation recovered three RCR parameters from synthetic data with about 0.3% error.
infographic.watch_item: Residual local-pressure biases remain, and robustness to noisy clinical data has not yet been established.
infographic.paper_title: A 3D PINN-Based Framework for Patient-Specific Pulmonary Hemodynamics Using Windkessel Models

title: Numerical Study of Flow and Cavitation in Single-Liquid Injectors with Sharp-Edged and Chamfered Orifice Inlets
authors: Shreyash Gulati, Sven R. Walsberg, Timothy W. Nearhood, Jeffrey D. Moore
abstract: In the current work, the investigators used Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) to investigate water flow and cavitation in single-liquid injectors with sharp-edged and chamfered orifice inlets. The k-ω Shear Stress Transport (SST) turbulence model was used along with the Zwart-Gerber-Belamri (ZGB) cavitation model and the Volume of Fluid (VOF) method. The CFD predictions for the volumetric flow rate were validated against existing experimental data for the sharp-edged and chamfered orifice inlets. Pressure drops ranging between 0.07 MPa and 0.59 MPa were considered along with orifice length-to-diameter ratios of 2, 5, and 10. Strong cavitation was observed for the sharp-edged orifice inlet cases with a length-to-diameter ratio of 5 and a pressure drop larger than 0.2 MPa. A hydraulic flip was observed for the sharp-edged orifice inlet with a length-to-diameter ratio of 5 and a pressure drop of 0.59 MPa, which was consistent with the findings from the previous experimental study. Cavitation inception was observed for the chamfered orifice inlet cases with a length-to-diameter ratio of 5 and pressure drops larger than 0.2 MPa. For the sharp-edged orifice inlet with orifice length-to-diameter ratios of 2 and 10, a strong cavitation was observed inside the orifice.

infographic.key_insight: In CFD predictions at L/D = 5, sharp-edged inlets showed strong cavitation above a 0.2 MPa pressure drop and hydraulic flip at 0.59 MPa, while chamfered inlets showed cavitation inception above 0.2 MPa.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Inlet geometry and orifice length-to-diameter ratio are important design variables for managing injector cavitation and flow behavior.
method: CFD of water flow through sharp-edged and chamfered single-liquid injector inlets.
k–ω SST turbulence model coupled with Zwart–Gerber–Belamri cavitation modeling and VOF.
Pressure drops of 0.07–0.59 MPa and orifice L/D ratios of 2, 5, and 10.
infographic.evidence_signal: Predicted volumetric flow rates were validated against existing experiments for both inlet types, and the sharp-edged L/D = 5 hydraulic flip agreed with prior experimental findings.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract reports no validation error metrics; flow-rate agreement alone does not establish accuracy of local vapor distributions.
infographic.paper_title: Numerical Study of Flow and Cavitation in Single-Liquid Injectors with Sharp-Edged and Chamfered Orifice Inlets

title: Scalable Modal Analysis of the Imperial Front Wing Flow Field
authors: Parv Khurana, Benet Eiximeno, Alexandra Liosi, Spencer Sherwin, Athanasios Chatzopoulos, Julien Hoessler
abstract: The aerodynamic performance of motorsport vehicles relies on understanding the unsteady flow dynamics around complex geometries at high Reynolds numbers. Extracting the dominant 3D coherent structures from high-fidelity simulations is often intractable due to the high dimensionality of the state-space, and standard modal decompositions, such as proper orthogonal decomposition (POD), do not give interpretable meaning to the temporal dynamics of the modes. This study demonstrates a scalable POD and Dynamic Mode Decomposition (DMD) method, implemented in the open-source pyLOM framework, that can identify coherent structures and their temporal dynamics in high-fidelity simulations of Formula 1 aerodynamics, specifically the Imperial Front Wing (IFW), a publicly available benchmark based on the McLaren MP4-17D, at Reynolds number $Re = 2.2 \times 10^5$. DMD is applied to large eddy simulation (LES) results of the flow field that is resolved using spectral/hp element method via Nektar++, producing $49.72 \times 10^6$ degrees of freedom at polynomial order p=4. The simulation captures four dominant vortical structures (endplate, canard, main, and footplate), with time-averaged force coefficients showing 2.24% and 2.87% differences in $C_L$ and $C_D$ compared to the reference data. DMD extracts the frequencies, amplitudes and damping ratios of the coherent structures, and modes at chord-based Strouhal numbers of 5.1, 7.5 and 9.3 are associated, through point-probe spectra, with the main-element laminar separation bubble, canard vortex core pulsation and endplate vortex meander, respectively. The DMD allows for both a model reduction technique and a compression scheme, here reducing approximately 6 TB of snapshots to 200 GB of modal data.

infographic.key_insight: Scalable DMD identifies dominant 3D flow structures and their temporal dynamics around a Formula 1 front wing while compressing approximately 6 TB of snapshots to 200 GB of modal data.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Linking coherent structures to characteristic frequencies can support aerodynamic diagnosis and reduced-order modeling of complex motorsport flows.
method: Simulate the Imperial Front Wing at Re = 2.2 × 10^5 using spectral/hp-element LES in Nektar++.
Apply scalable POD and DMD through the open-source pyLOM framework.
Associate DMD modes with flow mechanisms using point-probe spectra.
infographic.evidence_signal: The simulation used 49.72 million degrees of freedom at polynomial order p = 4, with mean lift and drag coefficients differing from reference data by 2.24% and 2.87%; spectral comparisons associated chord-based Strouhal numbers 5.1, 7.5 and 9.3 with distinct flow mechanisms.
infographic.watch_item: Validation is reported for one geometry and Reynolds number; transferability to other operating conditions remains unestablished.
infographic.paper_title: Scalable Modal Analysis of the Imperial Front Wing Flow Field

title: Measuring and Improving Transfer of Neural Surrogates for Vehicle Aerodynamics
authors: Favour Nerrise, Julian Busch, Gurpreet Singh Hora, Martin Sipka, Danielle C. Maddix, Georgia Olympia Brikis
abstract: Neural surrogates for external vehicle aerodynamics are fast alternatives to physics-based computational fluid dynamics (CFD) simulations. Their foundational limitation is a lack of zero-shot generalization across vehicle classes, which results in an expensive, custom training campaign for each new vehicle design. Similar to pretrained models in other fields, a pretrained surrogate should adapt to a new vehicle class using only a few simulations and stay accurate on its pretraining domain. No prior study has systematically tested this transfer behavior. We conduct a large-scale, controlled benchmarking study on five DrivAerML-pretrained surrogates across four independent target datasets. These datasets differ from the source in geometry, CFD solver, turbulence model, and flow conditions. We find that fine-tuning these surrogates outperforms training from scratch in fewer than half of the comparisons and lowers the accuracy of the surrogate on its source dataset. We introduce GeoReplay, a geometry- and gradient-aligned source replay that keeps source simulations resembling the target in training and applies their updates only when they agree with the target gradient. A risk bound separates geometric coverage from differences in the simulated physics, and we prove that every sufficiently small GeoReplay step decreases the target training objective. GeoReplay lowers the source error of fine-tuning in 77 of 80 settings and matches its target accuracy.

infographic.key_insight: Pretrained vehicle-aerodynamics surrogates transfer unreliably, while GeoReplay preserves source-domain accuracy without sacrificing fine-tuning’s target accuracy.
infographic.engineering_relevance: GeoReplay could make surrogate adaptation to new vehicle classes more reusable while limiting loss of accuracy on previously modeled vehicles.
method: Benchmark five DrivAerML-pretrained surrogates on four independent target datasets.
Replay source simulations with geometries resembling the target, applying their updates only when aligned with the target gradient.
Separate geometric coverage from simulated-physics differences in a risk bound and prove target-training descent for sufficiently small GeoReplay steps.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across datasets differing in geometry, CFD solver, turbulence model, and flow conditions, fine-tuning beat training from scratch in fewer than half of comparisons; GeoReplay reduced fine-tuning’s source error in 77 of 80 settings while matching target accuracy.
infographic.watch_item: GeoReplay requires retained source simulations and gradient-alignment checks; its target-training descent guarantee does not establish generalization to unseen vehicles.
infographic.paper_title: Measuring and Improving Transfer of Neural Surrogates for Vehicle Aerodynamics

title: Failure Modes and Data-Efficient Remedies for Transformer-Based Prediction of Viscoplastic Flows
authors: Maedeh Saberi, Hugo Franca, Maziyar Jalaal, Safa Jamali
abstract: Fast and accurate prediction of viscoplastic flows remains a challenge in computational rheology due to yield surfaces, discontinuous gradients, and strongly nonlinear transitions between yielded and unyielded regions. Transformer-based neural operators such as RheOFormer have recently shown strong potential for surrogate modeling of non-Newtonian flows. However, their applicability to viscoplastic systems and their efficacy in recovering realistic flows remain poorly understood. In this work, we present the first systematic investigation of RheOFormer applied to steady Bingham channel flow. By isolating the problem to a simple geometry and constitutive model, we examine how dataset structure, numerical value range, and input representation govern the model's ability to interpolate and extrapolate within the parameter space. The data regimes in which RheOFormer remains accurate and those in which errors emerge are identified, particularly for plug-dominated flows and for conditions outside the velocity scales or flow structures represented during training. Upon identifying these failure modes, targeted enhancements to the input representation and loss formulation are introduced to better predict low-gradient plug regions. Logarithmic velocity representations and gradient-aware loss formulations substantially improve accuracy in challenging regimes where the baseline formulation fails. In addition, extrapolation errors are reduced by augmenting the training set with only a few strategically selected cases spanning the missing physical regimes. Finally, a single partially developed snapshot suffices for an accurate steady-state prediction, and the model outperforms simply copying its input throughout flow development. These results highlight the importance of appropriate field representation and parameter-space coverage for data-efficient neural-operator prediction of viscoplastic flows.

infographic.key_insight: RheOFormer’s failures in viscoplastic flow prediction can be mitigated with logarithmic velocity representations, gradient-aware losses, and a few strategically selected training cases.
infographic.engineering_relevance: These remedies support more data-efficient CFD surrogates for yield-stress fluids, particularly in low-gradient plug regions and underrepresented flow regimes.
method: Evaluate RheOFormer on steady Bingham channel flow across dataset structures, value ranges, and input representations.
Use logarithmic velocity representations and gradient-aware losses to improve plug-region predictions.
Add a few cases covering missing physical regimes to reduce extrapolation errors.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports improved accuracy in challenging regimes, reduced extrapolation errors, and accurate steady-state prediction from one partially developed snapshot, outperforming input copying.
infographic.watch_item: Evidence is limited to a simple channel geometry and Bingham constitutive model; transfer to complex geometries or other rheologies remains unestablished.
infographic.paper_title: Failure Modes and Data-Efficient Remedies for Transformer-Based Prediction of Viscoplastic Flows

title: Stable eigenmodes of the Large-scale circulation in Turbulent Convection
authors: Yin Wang, Pik-Yin Lai, Penger Tong
abstract: Turbulent Rayleigh-Bénard convection (RBC) is a canonical system for studying buoyancy-driven turbulence. Its defining feature is a system-size large-scale circulation (LSC), whose dynamics reflect the coupling between coherent motion and turbulent fluctuations. Starting from the Boussinesq Navier-Stokes and temperature equations, we derive three coupled stochastic equations for the LSC angular velocity and its associated dipolar temperature field. The deterministic dynamics contain an unstable no-LSC set and two symmetry-related stable finite-LSC states. Linearization about either finite-LSC state yields one purely relaxational eigenmode and a pair of damped oscillatory eigenmodes whose frequency is set by the LSC turnover rate. Turbulent fluctuations continually excite the latter, providing a dynamical origin for the observed quasi-periodic oscillations. Experiments in a thin-disk cell directly resolve both eigenmodes and show their predicted Rayleigh-number scalings. The same stochastic dynamics also provide a route to rare cessations and reversals. This theory-experiment framework provides a tractable example of how coherent circulation states, intrinsic modes, and fluctuation-driven transitions emerge in turbulent convection, with broader relevance to geophysical and astrophysical flows.

infographic.key_insight: A three-variable stochastic model explains how stable large-scale circulation supports a relaxational mode and damped oscillatory modes continually excited by turbulence.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The model offers a reduced-order framework for understanding coherent circulation, oscillations, and rare flow reversals in buoyancy-driven systems.
method: Derive coupled stochastic equations for circulation angular velocity and a dipolar temperature field from the Boussinesq equations.
Linearize around stable finite-circulation states to identify relaxation and oscillation modes.
Compare predicted modes and Rayleigh-number scalings with thin-disk convection experiments.
infographic.evidence_signal: Thin-disk experiments resolve the relaxational and oscillatory modes and show their predicted Rayleigh-number scalings.
infographic.watch_item: Validation described in the abstract is limited to a thin-disk cell; applicability to other geometries and quantitative prediction of rare transitions need further testing.
infographic.paper_title: Stable eigenmodes of the Large-scale circulation in Turbulent Convection

title: A centered finite-volume method with explicit pressure relaxation for weakly compressible single- and two-phase flows
authors: Shintaro Matsushita, Suhas S. Jain, Andrei G. Fedorov, Tetsuya Suekane
abstract: We present a non-dissipative centered finite-volume method for weakly compressible single- and two-phase flows. The method couples kinetic-energy-preserving advection to conservative diffuse-interface regularization and explicit pressure relaxation on structured collocated grids. To control excessive phase-mass outflow when neighboring cells have different intrinsic densities, we construct phase-mass fluxes using harmonic face densities. This connects phase-volume and phase-mass transport without altering the advective kinetic-energy identity, yielding a sufficient positivity condition and an inverse-density transport identity at finite velocity divergence. To retain the benefit of low-dissipation transport in the coupled calculation, a pressure-increment formulation incorporates the existing pressure gradient in the predictor. Compatible cell and face operators give a conditional energy estimate for additional pressure iterations, while fully discrete budgets separate advection, predictor pressure work, and the final correction. In inviscid homogeneous isotropic turbulence on $128^3$ cells, the relative kinetic-energy change remains below $1.2\times10^{-7}$ in magnitude at $t^*=8$ in both single-phase and density-ratio-$1000$ two-phase calculations. Matched upwind calculations retain only $3.60\%$ and $30.72\%$ of their initial energies, respectively. Shear layers, cavities, rising bubbles, and dam breaks demonstrate applicability to incompressible-regime flows. In a three-dimensional dam break, harmonic averaging retains positive phase masses where arithmetic averaging produces negative values. With centered advection, a prescribed subgrid-scale stress supplies the principal dissipation. The local pressure algorithm and collocated finite-volume form support future large-scale multiphase large-eddy simulation on GPUs with adaptive mesh refinement.

infographic.key_insight: Centered finite-volume transport with explicit pressure relaxation nearly preserves kinetic energy in weakly compressible single- and two-phase flows, while harmonic face densities help maintain positive phase masses.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The low-dissipation, collocated formulation offers a foundation for multiphase large-eddy simulation, with future GPU and adaptive-mesh implementations in view.
method: Couple kinetic-energy-preserving centered advection with conservative diffuse-interface regularization.
Use harmonic face densities to link phase-volume and phase-mass transport.
Apply pressure-increment relaxation with compatible cell and face operators.
infographic.evidence_signal: In inviscid turbulence on 128³ cells, relative kinetic-energy changes stayed below 1.2×10⁻⁷ in magnitude at t*=8 for single-phase and density-ratio-1000 two-phase cases; matched upwind runs retained only 3.60% and 30.72% of initial energy, respectively.
infographic.watch_item: Phase-mass positivity and pressure-iteration energy estimates are conditional; GPU and adaptive-mesh scalability remain future work.
infographic.paper_title: A centered finite-volume method with explicit pressure relaxation for weakly compressible single- and two-phase flows

title: Compressibility effects on the flow-induced motions of bluff bodies: common features from transverse and rotary oscillations
authors: Sawant Omkar Deepak, Swagata Bhaumik
abstract: Compressibility effects on flow-induced motions of bluff bodies are examined through two-dimensional direct numerical simulations of undamped transverse vortex-induced vibration (TVIV) of a circular cylinder ($Re=150$) and vortex-induced rotary oscillation (VIRO) of an elliptic cylinder of aspect ratio $0.5$ ($Re=200$) for free-stream Mach numbers $0.1\leq M_{\infty}\leq 0.6$. Response characteristics are analyzed across the first desynchronized zone ($DS\text{-}I$), the synchronous (lock-in) branch ($SB$), and the second desynchronized zone ($DS\text{-}II$). While compressibility effects are noted to stabilize the oscillations in $SB$ in terms of reductions in response amplitudes and fluctuating aerodynamic coefficients, as well as the extent and intensity of hysteretic jumps, in contrast, the oscillation amplitudes and aerodynamic coefficients increase with $M_{\infty}$ in $DS\text{-}II$, where the amplitude variation with $M_{\infty}$ is shown to follow the \textit{modified Prandtl-Glauert relationship} for both TVIV and VIRO cases. This indicates the role of the inviscid nature of compressibility in the $DS\text{-}II$ regime in increasing the oscillation response, as opposed to $SB$ where enhanced viscous stabilization with increasing $M_{\infty}$ leads to the moderation of response. Although the simulations are performed at low Reynolds numbers, the identified trends are consistent with fundamental compressibility mechanisms and may therefore persist at higher Reynolds numbers.

infographic.key_insight: Increasing compressibility suppresses bluff-body oscillations during lock-in but amplifies them in the second desynchronized regime, revealing a shared response across transverse and rotary motions.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Compressibility can either moderate or intensify flow-induced motion, so vibration assessments must account for the body's synchronization regime.
method: Two-dimensional direct numerical simulations at free-stream Mach numbers 0.1–0.6.
Undamped transverse vibration of a circular cylinder at Re = 150 and rotary oscillation of an elliptic cylinder at Re = 200 with aspect ratio 0.5.
Comparison across first desynchronized, synchronous lock-in, and second desynchronized regimes.
infographic.evidence_signal: Simulations show reduced amplitudes, fluctuating aerodynamic coefficients, and hysteretic jumps during lock-in, while second-desynchronized amplitudes increase with Mach number following a modified Prandtl–Glauert relationship in both cases.
infographic.watch_item: The findings come from two-dimensional, low-Reynolds-number simulations; persistence at higher Reynolds numbers remains unverified.
infographic.paper_title: Compressibility effects on the flow-induced motions of bluff bodies: common features from transverse and rotary oscillations

title: Discrete adjoint method for the general synthetic iterative scheme for optimization of rarefied and continuum gas flows
authors: Jianan Zeng, Ruifeng Yuan, Wei Su
abstract: A discrete adjoint method is developed for the general synthetic iterative scheme (GSIS) to enable efficient gradient-based optimization of gas flows across rarefied and continuum regimes. The primal GSIS is expressed as a fixed-point system of kinetic and macroscopic synthetic equations, and both sets of residuals are incorporated into a discrete Lagrangian. Imposing stationarity of this Lagrangian then yields a coupled mesoscopic-macroscopic adjoint system that directly inherits the primal acceleration structure, without a separate Chapman-Enskog or asymptotic analysis. The resulting system is solved by alternating kinetic and macroscopic updates analogous to those in the primal GSIS, with the inner subproblems treated using established discrete adjoint techniques for the discrete velocity method and Navier-Stokes equations. Tests on the NACA0012 airfoil show that adjoint sensitivities closely agree with central finite-difference estimates, while the adjoint solver achieves convergence efficiency comparable to that of the primal GSIS, with both solvers converging within tens of iterations in rarefied and near-continuum flows. The method is further validated by multi-objective shape optimization and boundary-flow-parameter optimization. For a three-dimensional re-entry capsule, shape optimization reduces peak wall heat flux by 14.17%, 10.68%, and 6.54% while achieving respective lift-to-drag gains of 10%, 20%, and 25%. For a fixed-geometry showerhead chamber, optimization of inlet-flow allocation reduces the coefficient of variation of wafer pressure from 1.49% to 0.06% at fixed total gas supply, while maintaining the mean pressure near its initial value. Beyond these applications, the formulation provides a systematic and extensible framework for constructing multiscale adjoint solvers directly from the fixed-point representations of their primal counterparts.

infographic.key_insight: A discrete adjoint built directly from GSIS enables efficient gradient-based gas-flow optimization across rarefied and continuum regimes while preserving the primal solver’s acceleration structure.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The method supports aerodynamic and thermal shape optimization and precise gas-flow allocation in manufacturing chambers.
method: Express kinetic and macroscopic GSIS equations as a fixed-point system.
Include both residual sets in a discrete Lagrangian to derive coupled adjoint equations.
Alternate kinetic and macroscopic adjoint updates using established discrete adjoint techniques.
infographic.evidence_signal: NACA0012 sensitivities closely match central finite differences with convergence in tens of iterations; capsule optimization reduces peak heat flux by 6.54–14.17%, while chamber optimization lowers wafer-pressure variation from 1.49% to 0.06%.
infographic.watch_item: Implementation requires consistent differentiation and coupling of both kinetic and macroscopic discrete residuals; broader performance beyond the reported cases remains unestablished.
infographic.paper_title: Discrete adjoint method for the general synthetic iterative scheme for optimization of rarefied and continuum gas flows

title: Oceanic Surface Waves from Wind-Drift-Layer Instability: Exponential Growth to Finite-Amplitude States
authors: Sayali N. Jadhav, S. Ravichandran, Ratul Dasgupta
abstract: Oceanic wind-wave genesis via shear-induced linear instability and the propagation and breaking of finite-amplitude waves have traditionally been studied as decoupled problems. While experimental evidence indicates connection between the two regimes, a first principles demonstration that the latter can emerge from the former remains challenging. Here, we bridge this gap by investigating gravity-dominated surface waves arising from an inviscid, shear-driven Holmboe instability. The background state comprises a uniform air current and a constant-vorticity water drift layer of finite thickness overlying deep irrotational water. In the high-Bond-number and low-Froude-number regime, this configuration supports Holmboe-unstable modes beyond a critical Froude number. Two-phase simulations of the incompressible Navier-Stokes equations, initialised with the fastest-growing eigenmode, exhibit initial exponential growth in excellent agreement with linear theory. In the subsequent nonlinear stage preceding breaking, finite-amplitude propagating waveforms develop. Spatio-temporal spectral analysis reveals bound harmonics locked to the primary carrier wave, coexisting with residual free-wave components. This indicates that an infinitesimal, linearly unstable mode can evolve into a nonlinear propagating waveform of approximately permanent form under background shear. To characterise these waveforms theoretically, we formulate an exact nonlinear boundary-value problem for steady-state propagating waves including background shear. The resulting wave profiles show very good agreement with time-averaged profiles extracted from the transient simulations in the nonlinear stage. These findings extend the existing theory and complement the wind-wave observations, demonstrating that sheared Stokes-like waves, can naturally emerge during the nonlinear evolution of a wind-drift-induced linear instability.

infographic.key_insight: A wind-drift-induced Holmboe instability can evolve from infinitesimal disturbances into finite-amplitude, propagating Stokes-like surface waves under background shear.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The results connect wave onset and nonlinear propagation in a framework relevant to physics-based modeling of wind-generated ocean waves.
method: Analyze linear instability of uniform airflow over a finite-thickness, constant-vorticity water layer and deep irrotational water.
Initialize two-phase incompressible Navier–Stokes simulations with the fastest-growing eigenmode.
Compare nonlinear wave spectra and profiles with an exact steady traveling-wave boundary-value formulation.
infographic.evidence_signal: Simulated early growth agrees excellently with linear theory, while pre-breaking spectra show carrier-locked bound harmonics and time-averaged wave profiles agree very well with nonlinear theory.
infographic.watch_item: The findings concern an idealized shear configuration in a high-Bond-number, low-Froude-number regime; applicability to realistic turbulent seas and breaking requires further validation.
infographic.paper_title: Oceanic Surface Waves from Wind-Drift-Layer Instability: Exponential Growth to Finite-Amplitude States

title: Flow-induced vibration of an array of circular cylinders in a square enclosure due to thermal buoyancy
authors: Amit Pramod Joshi, Nishit Gupta, Unnat Agarwal, Vaibhav Joshi
abstract: Flow-induced oscillations of heated cylinder arrays in a square enclosure driven solely by natural convection are investigated in the current study at Prandtl number of 7 and Raleigh number of $10^7$ (based on side of square enclosure). This is accomplished by a coupled thermal-fluid-structure-interaction formulation based on body-fitted arbitrary Lagrangian-Eulerian framework, implemented using variational finite element methodology. Study on stationary array shows asymmetry in the $3\times 3$ configuration, along with a non-dimensional wall-gap plume oscillation frequency of 0.183 on the left column cylinders. When elastically mounted, these cylinders synchronize and lock-in with the frequency at reduced velocity of 15.7. The remaining cylinders undergo broadband buffeting that grows monotonically with reduced velocity and exceeds the synchronized response. The $4\times 4$ array shows symmetric behavior with no synchronization. The response is observed to be forced buffeting for all the cylinders, and dominated by the slow plume forcing for the inner column cylinders. The motion of the cylinders also influence the heat transfer characteristics. The $3\times 3$ array shows negligible change in heat transfer for the whole array, while measurable enhancement is observed for $4\times 4$ array.

infographic.key_insight: Buoyancy-driven flow synchronizes selected cylinders in a 3×3 array, whereas a 4×4 array exhibits forced buffeting without synchronization.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Cylinder-array layout can alter vibration and heat transfer in naturally cooled tube bundles, making thermal and structural performance important to assess together.
method: Simulate heated cylinder arrays in a square enclosure at Pr = 7 and Ra = 10⁷.
Couple thermal, fluid, and structural dynamics using a body-fitted arbitrary Lagrangian–Eulerian finite-element formulation.
Compare stationary and elastically mounted 3×3 and 4×4 arrays.
infographic.evidence_signal: The 3×3 left-column cylinders lock in to a nondimensional plume frequency of 0.183 at reduced velocity 15.7; array-wide heat transfer changes negligibly for 3×3 but increases measurably for 4×4.
infographic.watch_item: Results are reported at one Prandtl–Rayleigh parameter pair, so broader operating-range applicability requires further evaluation.
infographic.paper_title: Flow-induced vibration of an array of circular cylinders in a square enclosure due to thermal buoyancy

title: AI Meets Turbulence Modeling: Balancing Causation, Correlation, and User Intent
authors: Sharath S. Girimaji
abstract: Turbulence states vary widely in modeling difficulty, requiring distinct paradigms; thus, no single AI or data-driven approach suits all flows. We propose an operational framework classifying data-driven turbulence modeling by balancing physical causation and statistical correlation via non-equilibrium flow memory and user intent. Using the Mori--Zwanzig projection formalism, we decompose unclosed turbulent stress into a local response ($τ_{ij}^L$) and a spatio-temporally non-local memory integral ($τ_{ij}^{NL}$). Near statistical equilibrium, rapid relaxation suppresses advective memory, letting local correlations capture physical causation via intrusive $τ_{ij}^L$ constitutive relations in Reynolds-Averaged Navier--Stokes (RANS) equations. Because the elliptic Poisson equation for fluctuating pressure couples stress evolution to eddy dimensionality beyond single-point velocity-gradient componentiality, local closures are not strictly valid even at equilibrium, yet remain acceptable engineering approximations. In non-equilibrium turbulence, modeling bifurcates by user intent. For predicting unseen geometries, large coherent structures sustain non-local memory ($τ_{ij}^{NL}$), invalidating local total-stress closures and requiring first-principles causal scale resolution guided by Rules-Augmented AI (RAAI), with resolution set by a recent non-equilibrium theory. Conversely, for rapid design in a known, parameterized coherent flow class, a purely correlational strategy suffices: combining Non-Intrusive Reduced-Order Modeling (NIROM) with uncentered Proper Orthogonal Decomposition (POD) across multi-realization ensembles yields zero-solver synthesis of stationary statistics and unsteady coherent evolution from governing dimensionless parameters. This framework aligns physical causation, statistical correlation, and user intent across flow regimes.

infographic.key_insight: AI turbulence modeling should balance physical causation and statistical correlation according to flow memory and user intent, rather than use one universal approach.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework guides engineers toward local RANS closures near equilibrium, causal scale resolution for unseen non-equilibrium flows, or fast surrogate synthesis within known flow classes.
method: Use Mori–Zwanzig projection to separate turbulent stress into local response and non-local memory.
For unseen non-equilibrium flows, use Rules-Augmented AI to guide first-principles scale resolution.
For known parameterized flow classes, combine non-intrusive reduced-order modeling with uncentered POD across multi-realization ensembles.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract presents a theoretical framework and ensemble-based modeling strategy but reports no quantitative benchmarks or validation metrics.
infographic.watch_item: Local closures remain approximate even at equilibrium because pressure introduces non-local coupling; purely correlational surrogates are intended for known, parameterized flow classes.
infographic.paper_title: AI Meets Turbulence Modeling: Balancing Causation, Correlation, and User Intent

title: Vortex rings shape the feeding-efficiency landscape of jellyfish
authors: Harry Walden, Ashutosh Tripathi, Teo Lara, Brandon Weissbourd, Jörn Dunkel
abstract: Fluid flows enable and limit the feeding and locomotion of sea creatures across a wide range of scales. Although much is known about how microorganisms navigate life at low Reynolds numbers, the effect of inertial flows on the feeding-efficiency of larger marine organisms remains less well understood. Here, using jellyfish as an archetypal example, we study the trade-off between prey capture rate and energy expended to generate inertial flows by surface deformations. We develop a feeding-efficiency landscape that predicts an optimal feeding regime at the transition from Stokes pumping to inertial prey transport, mediated by a self-generated vortex ring. These predictions provide a unifying biophysical explanation of size and beat frequencies reported for jellyfish species from different taxa, with vortex-ring-dominated transport supported by our experimental observations for the moon jellyfish \textit{Aurelia aurita}. More broadly, our results demonstrate how centimetric marine predators can exploit inertial flows for efficient prey capture.

infographic.key_insight: Jellyfish feeding efficiency is predicted to peak at the transition from Stokes pumping to inertial prey transport, where self-generated vortex rings enhance prey capture.
infographic.engineering_relevance: These findings could inform bio-inspired underwater pumps and robots that balance fluid transport against actuation energy.
method: Study prey capture versus energy spent deforming the jellyfish surface.
Develop a feeding-efficiency landscape spanning viscous and inertial transport.
Compare predictions with reported species traits and moon jellyfish observations.
infographic.evidence_signal: Predictions explain reported jellyfish sizes and beat frequencies across taxa, while observations of Aurelia aurita support vortex-ring-dominated transport.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract provides no quantitative validation metrics, and experimental support is reported only for moon jellyfish.
infographic.paper_title: Vortex rings shape the feeding-efficiency landscape of jellyfish

title: A shock-fitting approach to high-order simulation of viscous hypersonic flows based on inviscid implicit shock tracking
authors: Huijing Dong, Alexander M. Perez Reyes, Matthew J. Zahr
abstract: This work presents a framework for computing viscous, shock-dominated flows at high Mach and Reynolds numbers in which the bow shock is located by inviscid implicit shock tracking and then treated as a boundary of the viscous computation. The high-order implicit shock tracking (HOIST) method is applied to the Euler equations on a coarse, shock-agnostic mesh to produce a shock-aligned mesh and the shock geometry; the elements upstream of the shock are discarded, the post-shock domain is remeshed to resolve the boundary layer, and the compressible Navier-Stokes equations are solved on it with a high-order interior penalty discontinuous Galerkin method, with the post-shock state prescribed along the shock boundary by the oblique shock relations. Because the shock structure is never resolved, the approach requires neither the extreme element compression nor the specialized formulations that fully coupled viscous shock tracking demands at these conditions; the tracking optimization is confined to the coarse inviscid mesh, and the viscous computation involves no mesh unknowns and no additional nonlinear stabilization. The framework is demonstrated on a Mach 10.6 axisymmetric blunt cone, a Mach 17.6 cylinder, and a Mach 5 sphere in three dimensions, with surface pressure and heat flux in good agreement with experimental measurements and reference computations.

infographic.key_insight: Locating the bow shock with inviscid tracking and treating it as a viscous-domain boundary enables high-order hypersonic simulations without resolving the shock structure.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework supports prediction of hypersonic surface pressure and heating while avoiding extreme shock-layer mesh compression and coupled viscous shock-tracking optimization.
method: Apply high-order implicit shock tracking (HOIST) to the Euler equations on a coarse mesh to locate and align the bow shock.
Discard upstream elements and remesh the post-shock domain to resolve the boundary layer.
Solve compressible Navier–Stokes equations with high-order interior penalty discontinuous Galerkin, prescribing shock-boundary states using oblique shock relations.
infographic.evidence_signal: Tests on a Mach 10.6 axisymmetric blunt cone, Mach 17.6 cylinder, and Mach 5 three-dimensional sphere showed surface pressure and heat flux in good agreement with experiments and reference computations.
infographic.watch_item: Using an inviscidly determined shock as a fixed viscous-domain boundary warrants validation where viscous effects substantially alter shock position or geometry.
infographic.paper_title: A shock-fitting approach to high-order simulation of viscous hypersonic flows based on inviscid implicit shock tracking

title: An Annular Spiral Construction for Anomalous Dissipation in the Forced Navier-Stokes Equations
authors: Changhong Li
abstract: Kolmogorov's 1941 theory of turbulence (K41) predicts that the rate of kinetic energy dissipation in a turbulent flow can remain positive as viscosity tends to zero. In 2023, Bruè and De Lellis used quasi-self-similar mixing to construct solutions of the forced three-dimensional Navier-Stokes equations exhibiting anomalous dissipation. In this paper, we show that anomalous dissipation can still occur for a flow with spiral geometry in an annulus. In the horizontal plane, we wind a radial segment into a two-turn spiral and then apply alternating shears. After each pair of shears, the image of the segment shares a subarc of positive length with the original spiral. We compare the vertical velocity with sine profiles whose angular period halves with each pair. After the horizontal flow stops, diffusion damps the final profile. By embedding this planar construction into the $(2+\frac{1}{2})$-dimensional framework, we obtain smooth solutions of the three-dimensional equations with the same smooth initial datum. For a sequence of viscosities tending to zero, their dissipation over a fixed subannulus and one vertical period has a uniform positive lower bound, and their forces converge in $C^α$ uniformly in time for every $0<α<1$. We use this spiral construction to produce solutions of the forced three-dimensional Navier-Stokes equations that exhibit anomalous dissipation.

infographic.key_insight: An annular spiral flow construction yields forced three-dimensional Navier–Stokes solutions whose energy dissipation stays uniformly positive along a sequence of viscosities tending to zero.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The construction provides a theoretical benchmark for studying how mixing can sustain energy dissipation at very low viscosity.
method: Wind a radial segment into a two-turn spiral, then apply alternating planar shears.
Track vertical velocity against sine profiles whose angular period halves after each shear pair, then let diffusion act.
Embed the planar construction in a (2+½)-dimensional framework to obtain smooth three-dimensional solutions with identical initial data.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports a mathematical positive lower bound on dissipation over a fixed subannulus and one vertical period, with forces converging uniformly in time in C^α for every 0<α<1.
infographic.watch_item: This is a specially constructed forced-flow result along a viscosity sequence, not a demonstration for generic turbulent flows or engineering geometries.
infographic.paper_title: An Annular Spiral Construction for Anomalous Dissipation in the Forced Navier-Stokes Equations

title: Nonpremixed Flames Near the Leading Edge of Parabolic Cylinders
authors: Vinicius M. Sauer, Jose M. Martinez
abstract: Nonpremixed flames in the forward stagnation region of porous cylinders are classically described by the first-order stagnation-point boundary layer, which neglects the effects of surface curvature and boundary-layer displacement. In the present work, the description is extended to second order for a porous parabolic cylinder using the method of matched asymptotic expansions. The flame is assumed to be a sheet detached from the porous wall with unity Lewis numbers, and the model accounts for thermal expansion and displacement of the entire reacting layer. The expansion is verified against laminar Navier-Stokes solutions of the same idealized problem, and in the resolved cases the two-term errors decrease approximately as the square of the expansion parameter. At Reynolds numbers typical of laboratory-scale burners, curvature and displacement move the flame away from the wall and reduce the scalar dissipation rate, wall shear, and wall heat flux, whereas the flame temperature changes little. These effects increase with injection, and displacement contributes more over a longer porous section. The second-order terms considerably reduce the errors of the first-order theory in the flame stand-off distance and the scalar dissipation rate.

infographic.key_insight: Second-order curvature and displacement corrections predict flames farther from porous parabolic walls, with lower scalar dissipation, wall shear, and wall heat flux but little temperature change.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The corrections improve flame stand-off and scalar-dissipation predictions at laboratory-burner Reynolds numbers, especially with stronger injection or longer porous sections.
method: Extend stagnation-point boundary-layer theory using matched asymptotic expansions.
Include curvature, thermal expansion, and displacement of the reacting layer.
Model a detached flame sheet with unity Lewis numbers.
infographic.evidence_signal: Comparison with laminar Navier–Stokes solutions showed approximately quadratic error reduction with the expansion parameter in resolved cases.
infographic.watch_item: Applicability beyond the idealized laminar, unity-Lewis-number flame-sheet setting requires further validation; this is an asymptotic model, not an AI surrogate.
infographic.paper_title: Nonpremixed Flames Near the Leading Edge of Parabolic Cylinders

title: Nonlinearly Causal General-Relativistic Superfluid Hydrodynamics: Simulating Vortex Dynamics in Neutron-Star Interiors
authors: Yuan Feng, Elias R. Most, Lorenzo Gavassino
abstract: Neutron stars provide a natural laboratory for superfluid matter under extreme conditions. Its nonlinear dynamics is central to pulsar glitches, their possible links to fast radio bursts, and tidal interactions in inspiralling binaries. We develop a general-relativistic superfluid hydrodynamics framework incorporating entrainment, vortex forces, and line energy, and derive, for the first time, necessary and sufficient conditions for nonlinear causality and strong hyperbolicity. We also show that commonly used dissipative, force-balanced formulations without line tension are generically ill-posed at short wavelengths because of the Donnelly-Glaberson instability. Exploiting the analogy between vortex arrays with tension and force-free electrodynamics, we recast vortex dynamics in terms of effective electric and magnetic fields and drift velocities. This motivates a new finite-volume scheme combining constrained transport of superfluid vorticity with implicit electric-field evolution, enabling stable numerical evolution of the full system. We validate the scheme using an exact solution to the relativistic superfluid Riemann problem and Kelvin-wave dispersion relations, among other tests. Finally, we simulate dynamical, global general-relativistic two-fluid neutron-star equilibria, validate their oscillation modes, and present the first simplified calculation of superfluid interior spin-down with prescribed vortex release and repinning. The resulting stationary state retains both a net twist in the vortex array and residual differential rotation of the superfluid. Our framework thus enables nonlinear numerical studies of general-relativistic superfluid dynamics in neutron-star interiors.

infographic.key_insight: A general-relativistic superfluid framework establishes necessary and sufficient conditions for nonlinear causality and strong hyperbolicity, enabling stable simulations of neutron-star vortex dynamics.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework provides a computational foundation for studying superfluid transport, rotational dynamics, and pulsar-glitch mechanisms in neutron-star interiors.
method: Model entrainment, vortex forces, and vortex line energy in relativistic two-fluid hydrodynamics.
Recast vortex dynamics using effective electric and magnetic fields inspired by force-free electrodynamics.
Combine finite-volume evolution with constrained transport of vorticity and implicit electric-field updates.
infographic.evidence_signal: Validation includes an exact relativistic superfluid Riemann solution, Kelvin-wave dispersion relations, and neutron-star oscillation modes; a simplified spin-down simulation retains vortex twist and residual differential rotation.
infographic.watch_item: Vortex release and repinning are prescribed in the spin-down example, limiting conclusions about self-consistent glitch dynamics.
infographic.paper_title: Nonlinearly Causal General-Relativistic Superfluid Hydrodynamics: Simulating Vortex Dynamics in Neutron-Star Interiors

title: Generation and characterization of unsteady inflows in a fan-vane wind tunnel
authors: Yutong Liu, Gang Hu, Hongwei Zhang
abstract: Wind-tunnel experiments often require inflows with specific combinations of turbulence intensity and integral length scale because both can influence the measured response. To broaden the range of attainable inflows, this study uses pseudorandom vane excitation to generate large-scale turbulence and examines how both quantities vary with the amplitude and spectral shape of the vane-angle command. In each test, the 15 servo-driven vanes downstream of a 768-fan array received the same angle command, and all fans operated at a common, constant duty cycle. Hot-wire measurements covered twenty heights and selected spanwise and downstream positions. At a fan-control duty cycle of 60%, increasing vane angular amplitude raised profile-mean turbulence intensity from 7.3% to 31.8% under periodic forcing and from 6.2% to 23.0% under pseudorandom forcing. With the normalized pseudorandom command spectrum held fixed, larger angular amplitudes increased the low-frequency share of velocity variance, accompanied by longer correlation times and larger integral scales. At a root-mean-square angular amplitude of 15 degrees, changing the command spectrum yielded profile-mean integral length scales of 0.88-1.67 m at similar turbulence intensities. The principal features of the velocity spectra persisted between 2 and 4 m downstream, while integral scales continued to change. Both forcing types exhibited middle-region minima in turbulence intensity and integral scale. Regional analysis of a representative pseudorandom case linked these minima to weaker low-frequency fluctuations and shorter correlation times. These findings provide a basis for selecting vane inputs according to the turbulence-intensity and integral-scale requirements of the intended test region.

infographic.key_insight: Pseudorandom vane forcing broadens attainable wind-tunnel turbulence, with command amplitude and spectral shape controlling turbulence intensity and integral length scale.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Vane inputs can be selected to better match the turbulence intensity and length-scale requirements of a test region.
method: Applied identical angle commands to 15 servo-driven vanes downstream of a 768-fan array operating at constant duty cycle.
Varied vane amplitude and pseudorandom command spectra, with periodic forcing for comparison.
Measured velocity using hot wires at 20 heights and selected spanwise and downstream positions.
infographic.evidence_signal: At 60% fan duty, increasing pseudorandom forcing amplitude raised profile-mean turbulence intensity from 6.2% to 23.0%; at 15° RMS amplitude, changing the command spectrum yielded integral scales of 0.88–1.67 m at similar intensities.
infographic.watch_item: Inflow properties vary spatially: middle-region minima and downstream changes in integral scale require characterization within the intended test region.
infographic.paper_title: Generation and characterization of unsteady inflows in a fan-vane wind tunnel

title: A Fitch-Based Wind Farm Parameterization for CM1: Implementation, Validation, and Impacts on Convection Initiation
authors: Jianxiang Li, Zhiyong Meng
abstract: We implement a Fitch-based wind farm parameterization in Cloud Model 1 (CM1), representing turbines as elevated momentum sinks and turbulent kinetic energy (TKE) sources within the rotor-swept layer, with optimizations for computational efficiency and parallel execution. Direct comparison with the Weather Research and Forecasting (WRF) model shows close agreement in the magnitude and spatial structure of wind-speed deficits and TKE enhancement. Diurnal simulations also capture the known dependence of boundary layer responses on atmospheric stability, further supporting the consistency of the implementation. Under stable conditions, the wind farm produces coherent spatial patterns in near-surface wind speed and temperature that extend well beyond the farm. In idealized simulations under conditions favorable for convection, large turbines promote convection initiation tens of kilometers downstream, earlier than in the no-farm simulation. Analysis identifies turbulent entrainment of warmer air across the boundary layer top as the dominant source of an elongated downstream warm band, with a smaller contribution from enhanced surface sensible heat flux. Secondary circulations develop across this warm band and provide sustained low-level lifting. A gravity wave generated by the wind farm supplies the initial vertical perturbation, which intensifies as it is advected downstream within an ascending branch of these circulations and develops into a localized deep convective updraft.

infographic.key_insight: A Fitch-based wind farm parameterization in CM1 shows how turbine-induced warming and circulations can promote earlier convection initiation tens of kilometers downstream.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The implementation enables simulations of wind farm impacts on boundary layer flow and convective development beyond the farm footprint.
method: Represent turbines as elevated momentum sinks and TKE sources within the rotor-swept layer.
Optimize the CM1 implementation for computational efficiency and parallel execution.
Evaluate against WRF and use diurnal and idealized convection simulations to investigate atmospheric responses.
infographic.evidence_signal: Comparisons with WRF show close agreement in wind-speed deficits and TKE enhancement, while diurnal simulations reproduce known stability-dependent boundary layer responses.
infographic.watch_item: The convection findings come from idealized simulations; the abstract reports no observational validation of downstream storm initiation.
infographic.paper_title: A Fitch-Based Wind Farm Parameterization for CM1: Implementation, Validation, and Impacts on Convection Initiation

title: Mass-conservative and phase-consistent transport of phase-confined scalars in front tracking
authors: Ayman Mazloum, Gabriele Gennari, Fabian Denner, Berend van Wachem
abstract: In front-tracking multiphase-flow simulations, the Lagrangian front defines the interface geometry and phase regions, while phase-confined scalars are transported independently on a fixed Eulerian mesh. This separation can make the scalar inconsistent with the tracked interface: even a conservative high-order scheme smears the scalar across the interface, leaks it into the other phase and distorts near-interface concentrations despite conserving total mass. We present a transport method that maintains consistency between the scalar and the tracked front while preserving global mass conservation. Instead of the cell-averaged concentration, the method transports the phase-averaged concentration, which is smooth across the interface. This concentration is obtained by dividing the cell-averaged concentration by the phase fraction, extended linearly across the interface and advected. The cell-averaged concentration is rebuilt by multiplying the transported concentration by the front's volume-preserving phase fraction. Because this rebuild can alter the total mass, a uniform shift of the phase-averaged concentration restores it. The method is compared with direct transport of the cell-averaged concentration by the same scheme in five three-dimensional cases: three drops (in translation, in a reversible vortex and with a localized source) and a rising bubble with and without dissolved surfactant. In the four cases without surfactant it reduces the error against the exact solution by more than a factor of ten at the finest resolution and converges faster for the drops. In the surfactant-laden bubble, direct transport leaks 5.5-24% of the surfactant into the wake, depending on resolution, whereas the proposed method keeps it in the bubble.

infographic.key_insight: Transporting phase-averaged concentration keeps scalars confined to the front-tracked phase while preserving total mass.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The method improves scalar fidelity in multiphase-flow simulations where leakage across interfaces can distort concentrations and surfactant effects.
method: Divide cell-averaged concentration by phase fraction, then linearly extend it across the interface and advect.
Rebuild cell-averaged concentration using the tracked front’s volume-preserving phase fraction.
Apply a uniform phase-averaged concentration shift to restore total mass.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across five 3D tests, the method reduced error by more than tenfold at the finest resolution in four non-surfactant cases and kept surfactant inside the bubble where direct transport leaked 5.5–24% into the wake.
infographic.watch_item: Implementation must carefully handle division by small phase fractions and assess how the uniform mass correction affects local concentrations.
infographic.paper_title: Mass-conservative and phase-consistent transport of phase-confined scalars in front tracking
